verses.text: A few days later Jesus went back to Capernaum. And when the people heard that He was home,
they gathered in such large numbers that there was no more room, not even outside the door, as Jesus spoke the word to them.
Then a paralytic was brought to Him, carried by four men.
Since they were unable to get to Jesus through the crowd, they uncovered the roof above Him, made an opening, and lowered the paralytic on his mat.
When Jesus saw their faith, He said to the paralytic, "Son, your sins are forgiven."
But some of the scribes were sitting there and thinking in their hearts,
"Why does this man speak like this? He is blaspheming! Who can forgive sins but God alone?"
At once Jesus knew in His spirit that they were thinking this way within themselves. "Why are you thinking these things in your hearts?" He asked.
"Which is easier: to say to a paralytic, 'Your sins are forgiven,' or to say, 'Get up, pick up your mat, and walk'?
But so that you may know that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins..." He said to the paralytic,
"I tell you, get up, pick up your mat, and go home."
And immediately the man got up, picked up his mat, and walked out in front of them all. As a result, they were all astounded and glorified God, saying, "We have never seen anything like this!"
Once again Jesus went out beside the sea. All the people came to Him, and He taught them there.
As He was walking along, He saw Levi son of Alphaeus sitting at the tax booth. "Follow Me," He told him, and Levi got up and followed Him.
While Jesus was dining at Levi's house, many tax collectors and sinners were eating with Him and His disciples—for there were many who followed Him.
When the scribes who were Pharisees saw Jesus eating with these people, they asked His disciples, "Why does He eat with tax collectors and sinners?"
On hearing this, Jesus told them, "It is not the healthy who need a doctor, but the sick. I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners."
Now John's disciples and the Pharisees were often fasting. So people came to Jesus and asked, "Why don't Your disciples fast like John's disciples and those of the Pharisees?"
Jesus replied, "How can the guests of the bridegroom fast while He is with them? As long as He is with them, they cannot fast.
But the time will come when the bridegroom will be taken from them; then they will fast.
No one sews a patch of unshrunk cloth on an old garment. If he does, the new piece will pull away from the old, and a worse tear will result.
And no one pours new wine into old wineskins. If he does, the wine will burst the skins, and both the wine and the wineskins will be ruined. Instead, new wine is poured into new wineskins."
One Sabbath Jesus was passing through the grainfields, and His disciples began to pick the heads of grain as they walked along.
So the Pharisees said to Him, "Look, why are they doing what is unlawful on the Sabbath?"
Jesus replied, "Have you never read what David did when he and his companions were hungry and in need?
During the high priesthood of Abiathar, he entered the house of God and ate the consecrated bread, which was lawful only for the priests. And he gave some to his companions as well."
Then Jesus declared, "The Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath.
Therefore, the Son of Man is Lord even of the Sabbath."

context.author: Traditionally John Mark, a companion of Peter
context.genre: Narrative Gospel — five short, tightly linked controversy stories, each ending with Jesus overturning a religious assumption
context.audience: Roman Christian readers watching Jesus' authority collide, again and again, with the religious establishment's expectations
context.setting: Capernaum again, likely at Peter's own house, packed so tightly that four men resort to digging through the roof. First-century Galilean homes used flat roofs made of branches, mud, and packed earth over wooden beams — genuinely possible to open up from above without structural danger.
context.custom: Pharisaic tradition had expanded fasting well beyond the Day of Atonement into a twice-weekly practice. Jesus' bridegroom imagery would have been immediately understood as a wedding metaphor — wedding guests were specifically exempted from fasting obligations during the celebration itself.
context.timelineImmediate: Five back-to-back conflict stories — forgiving sins, eating with sinners, skipping fasts, and two separate Sabbath disputes — building toward the Pharisees' and Herodians' plot to kill Jesus that opens chapter 3.
context.timelineBible: Jesus' claim to forgive sins directly invokes Isaiah 43:25, where God alone declares "I, even I, am He who blots out your transgressions" — the scribes' objection in v.7 is theologically correct on its own terms, which is exactly what makes Jesus' claim so pointed.
context.sparkNotes: Four friends dig through a roof to lower a paralyzed man to Jesus, who forgives his sins before healing him — a deliberate order that provokes the scribes' unspoken charge of blasphemy. The chapter closes with Jesus and the Pharisees clashing over the Sabbath itself, ending in His boldest claim yet: "the Son of Man is Lord even of the Sabbath."

translation.meaning: Implies a release or letting go — the same verb family used elsewhere for canceling a debt.

occurrences.note: This broader root covers "leave," "let go," and "forgive" alike — only around a third of its uses are specifically about forgiving sin.

translation.greek: ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ ἀνθρώπου (ho huios tou anthropou)
translation.meaning: Jesus' favorite self-designation throughout Mark, appearing here for the first time — it draws on Daniel 7's vision of a figure given everlasting dominion, while sounding humble on the surface.
Fresh and unprecedented, not merely "another one" — Jesus' two short parables both stress that what He brings can't simply be patched onto the old system.

gospelParallels.note: Matthew's parallel account covering the same five episodes in the same order.
Luke's version, with added detail on the physicians the bleeding woman had exhausted her funds on.

otBackground.note: God alone blots out transgressions — the theological principle behind the scribes' objection in v.7.
David eating the consecrated bread when hungry — the precedent Jesus cites directly in v.25-26.
The Sabbath's origin at creation and its place in the Ten Commandments — background for Jesus' claim of Lordship over it.

commentary.note: Henry reads Jesus' choice to forgive before healing as deliberate: "pardon of sin strikes at the root of all diseases," since sin is, in his words, the true disease of the soul. The physical healing becomes almost secondary — a visible sign of the deeper, invisible work Jesus had already done.

JFB notes something easy to miss: all three Gospel accounts specifically say Jesus saw "their faith" — not just the paralyzed man's, but his four friends' as well. It was a shared, active faith, one that pushed through a crowded doorway and tore open a roof rather than accepting defeat.

Calvin frames the whole miracle as a kind of proof by demonstration — since forgiveness itself can't be visibly tested, Christ intentionally paired His invisible claim to forgive sins with a visible, undeniable sign (the healing) to confirm and seal an authority that could otherwise only be taken on faith.

Lewis does not comment on Mark 2, but "The Shocking Alternative" in Mere Christianity centers on Jesus' words to the paralytic, "Your sins are forgiven" (v.5-10). Lewis says that anyone can forgive a wrong done to himself, but a man who forgives wrongs done to other people is making an absurd claim unless he is the one whom every sin offends. So the claim to forgive sins is part of why Jesus cannot be reduced to a good teacher. (Paraphrased; Lewis's works remain under copyright.)

overview.summary: Four friends lower a paralyzed man through a roof, and Jesus forgives and heals him. He eats with tax collectors, is asked about fasting, and says the Son of Man is Lord even of the Sabbath.

history.t: They worked for Rome and were hated as collaborators who took extra.
Some Pharisees fasted twice a week, a practice beyond the Law.

customs.t: Roofs of beams, branches and clay could be opened from above.
Old skins grew stiff and would burst if filled with fermenting wine.

archaeology.t: Capernaum houses were small basalt homes around shared courtyards.
Customs stations stood along the lakeshore road near Capernaum.

overview.discussion: Jesus forgave the man's sins before healing him. Why might forgiveness have been the bigger need?
